title: Do not trade away a required key without an intentional Act 3 plan
situation: When offered a choice between a colored key and a linked relic, especially if the run is still pursuing the full-key route.
lesson: Take the Sapphire Key unless deliberately abandoning the Act 3 key objective. A useful relic is not worth permanently losing access to the corresponding key path when the run may otherwise survive to Act 3.
evidence_points: Act 1 Floor 9: the run chose Meat on the Bone and gave up the Sapphire Key.
Act 2 Floor 26: the run again chose Dream Catcher and gave up the Sapphire Key.
The final keys were ruby=True, emerald=False, sapphire=False.
reasoning: Both key opportunities were declined, so the run was guaranteed to finish without the Sapphire Key regardless of later combat performance. This is a reusable planning error rather than merely a symptom of the final loss.

title: Stop adding marginal attacks once the damage package is established
situation: When the deck already contains several efficient attacks and later rewards offer another copy or upgrade with limited defensive or scaling value.
lesson: Prefer skipping redundant damage rewards or taking cards that improve defense, scaling, or exhaust consistency. In particular, reassess duplicate Angers, Thunderclaps, and Perfected Strikes instead of continuing to enlarge an already attack-heavy deck.
evidence_points: The run took Carnage, Perfected Strike, Anger, another Anger+, Thunderclap, and Perfected Strike+ across the run.
The final 30-card deck still contained three Strikes, two Perfected Strikes including Perfected Strike+, Anger, Anger+, and Thunderclap.
Act 2 combat attrition was severe: HP fell from 89 after Floor 21 combat to 21 after Floor 23 combat, then to 15 after Floor 24 combat.
reasoning: The final build had a substantial damage package, yet the deck continued accepting marginal attack additions while losing most of its HP in consecutive Act 2 fights. Once damage is sufficient, reward decisions should address survivability and consistency rather than further increasing redundant attack density.

title: Do not spend the opening turn entirely on defense when the enemy board is still healthy
situation: When starting a fight at low HP against several enemies, especially when attacks are incoming, compare full-block lines against immediately weakening or killing one target.
lesson: Avoid automatically chaining every defensive card on turn one. In the final fight, Power Through, Shrug It Off, and Defend consumed all three energy without damaging an enemy; prefer a legal damage or debuff line when it can reduce the number or severity of future attacks, unless the state clearly requires full defense.
evidence_points: Turn 1 began at 18/80 HP with three enemies present, including two with ATTACK intent and Taskmaster with ATTACK_DEBUFF intent.
The chosen sequence was Power Through, Shrug It Off, and Defend, leaving all enemies at full HP; after ending the turn, player HP was 14/80.
On turn 2, all three enemies showed ATTACK_DEBUFF intent, while the first damaging play was not made until Pommel Strike.
reasoning: The log establishes that the all-defense line did not remove or weaken any enemy before the next enemy actions and cost 4 HP immediately. The exact best counterfactual is not fully recoverable, but the reusable correction is to avoid zero-damage openings when a low-HP fight has multiple active enemies and legal offensive alternatives.

title: Keep the Pyramid deck tighter and prioritize exhaust or hand control
situation: After obtaining Runic Pyramid, evaluate every additional card by whether it improves a retained hand or helps remove dead cards and generated wounds.
lesson: With Runic Pyramid, favor skip/removal and reliable exhaust or hand-management tools over broadly adding more cards. A large retained hand can preserve Wounds and dilute the important cards needed to stabilize a turn.
evidence_points: Runic Pyramid was chosen as the Act 1 boss relic.
The final deck contained 28 cards, including four Strikes and four Defends, while only one Strike was removed at the Act 1 shop.
In the final combat, the hand contained multiple Wounds; True Grit+ was used to select a Wound for exhaust, showing that retained clutter was an active problem.
reasoning: Pyramid makes dead cards persist rather than naturally leaving the hand at turn end. The final build and combat state both show that the deck still contained substantial basic-card density and generated Wounds, so future additions should be more selective and should improve exhaust, draw, or hand quality.

title: Protect an HP buffer before continuing Act 1 fights or taking marginal upgrades
situation: When repeated combats have reduced HP into the teens or low twenties, treat survival margin as the primary resource before choosing further combat paths or a smith.
lesson: Do not rely on late healing to recover from a long sequence of low-HP combats. After reaching very low HP, prioritize a recovery opportunity when available and only smith when the remaining HP buffer can safely support the next fights and boss.
evidence_points: The run began the first combat at 56/80 HP after taking the Neow damage option, then reached 21/80 by Act 1 Floor 8 and 13/80 by Floor 11.
The run did rest at 13/80 on Floor 12, but later chose smith at 23/80 on Floor 15 before the Act 1 boss.
The Hexaghost fight began at 23/80 and ended with the player at 22/80, while Act 2 later reached the final combat at 18/80.
reasoning: Although the run survived the boss, the repeated low-HP states left little margin for ordinary combat variance and made the final Act 2 fights much less forgiving. The lesson is to convert early damage and subsequent attrition into a deliberate recovery plan rather than treating each campfire upgrade as safe at low HP.

title: Convert low-HP campfires into recovery before the boss
situation: When approaching an Act boss at moderate or low HP and the deck already has several upgraded attacks, especially if a future elite or boss fight is unavoidable.
lesson: Prefer resting over smithing when the extra upgrade is unlikely to compensate for the risk of entering the boss damaged. Preserve enough HP to survive a bad draw and maintain defensive options during the boss fight.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 15, the player had 52/80 HP and chose smith, upgrading Shrug It Off instead of resting.
The Act 1 boss fight began at 52/80 HP and ended with the player at 6/80 HP.
At Act 1 Floor 16, the player was already at 12/80 HP when taking Immolate before the boss reward.
reasoning: The run repeatedly used campfires for upgrades despite steadily losing HP, and the resulting low boss-entry HP left almost no margin for combat variance. This supports treating recovery as the higher-value choice once HP is threatening the next major fight.

title: At critical HP, satisfy the attack before adding optional damage
situation: During a boss turn when HP is very low, the enemy has an attack intent, and the hand contains multiple defensive cards alongside attacks.
lesson: First spend energy on enough legal block to survive the known attack as far as the available state permits; only then use attacks or setup cards. Do not assume that ending with a small amount of block is acceptable when HP is already near death.
evidence_points: On Turn 11, the player had 16/80 HP, The Champ had ATTACK intent, and the player began with 4 energy.
After playing Battle Trance, the player spent energy on two Defends, then Pommel Strike and Wild Strike, ending the logged sequence with only 6 block.
The run ultimately ended in the Champ fight with the player dead while The Champ still had 43/420 HP.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not logged, so the precise lethal counterfactual cannot be proven. However, the sequence shows a critical-HP attack turn where defensive resources were not clearly prioritized over additional damage; future play should treat survival as the first constraint in this state.

title: Avoid overcommitting to early damage before defensive needs are met
situation: In early Act 1 rewards, when the deck already contains several attacks but has limited reliable block or draw, and future fights will require sustained defense.
lesson: After acquiring enough early damage to clear hallway enemies, favor efficient block, draw, or scaling over additional low-cost attacks unless the new attack fills a specific damage or matchup gap.
evidence_points: The first five Act 1 card rewards taken were Wild Strike, Twin Strike, Cleave, Carnage, and Pommel Strike.
The final 25-card deck still contained many attack cards, while its defensive additions were mainly Defends, Ghostly Armor, Iron Wave, Shrug It Off cards, True Grit, Flame Barrier, and Disarm+.
The Act 1 Floor 14 combat reduced HP from 55/80 to 46/80, and the Act 1 boss combat reduced it from 52/80 to 6/80.
reasoning: The early reward pattern heavily emphasized immediate attacks, while the run continued losing substantial HP in multi-enemy and boss fights. The lesson is not to reject attacks categorically, but to stop adding them once damage is adequate and prioritize cards that improve survival and consistency.

title: Prefer immediate preparation over late Girya scaling
situation: At a pre-boss campfire with Coffee Dripper and reduced HP, especially when smith is available alongside lift or dig.
lesson: Prioritize an immediate card upgrade or other boss-relevant preparation over a long-term strength option when there is no reliable healing and the next fight is imminent. Girya strength is valuable, but it does not repair a fragile defensive setup for the upcoming boss.
evidence_points: Act 2 Floor 32: HP 40/87, Coffee Dripper active, and both smith and lift were legal; lift was chosen.
Act 2 Floor 33 began the Automaton fight at 40/87 HP and ended with the player at 15/87 HP while the Automaton still had 229/300 HP.
reasoning: The chosen lift provided no immediate survivability before the boss, and the following fight showed both severe HP pressure and limited damage progress. With Coffee Dripper preventing normal rest healing, this was a particularly important opportunity to improve the deck before combat.

title: Price curse-risk events against available removal
situation: When an event offers a relic at a substantial curse risk and the run has limited gold or no guaranteed removal route.
lesson: Do not take a curse-risk relic event automatically; include the likely downstream removal cost in the decision. If the relic's value is uncertain and the run cannot comfortably absorb a curse, leaving can preserve both gold and deck quality.
evidence_points: Act 2 Floor 21: the Coffin event offered a relic with a 50% chance to become cursed, and Open Coffin was chosen.
Act 2 Floor 28: the run later spent 63 gold to remove Writhe.
reasoning: The event created a concrete downstream cost: the curse was later removed at a high shop price. The relic's identity and value are not recorded, so this is not proof that leaving was always correct, but it demonstrates why the curse probability and future removal burden must be evaluated together.

title: Treat self-damage as an emergency option at critical HP
situation: During a boss turn when HP is already low and Bloodletting is optional rather than required to produce lethal damage or enough block.
lesson: At critical HP, use Bloodletting only when its extra energy has a clear, necessary purpose; otherwise favor the legal non-self-damaging attacks, block, or ending the turn. Preserve HP for the next enemy action rather than converting it into marginal extra damage.
evidence_points: Final combat Turn 6: the player had 18/87 HP, an attacking Automaton, and legal alternatives including Defend+, attacks, Bloodletting+, and End turn.
Bloodletting+ was chosen after defensive cards, and the next logged state showed HP reduced to 15/87 before the remaining attacks were played; the Automaton was still at 235/300 HP at that point.
reasoning: The log confirms that Bloodletting directly consumed HP during an already dangerous boss turn, while the subsequent sequence still left the Automaton far from defeated. The exact incoming damage is unavailable, so this is a cautious sequencing lesson rather than proof that Bloodletting alone caused the loss.

title: Prefer preserving survivability over an uncertain max-HP penalty
situation: At Neow or similar early events, when the alternative is removing a card, evaluate whether an uncertain relic is worth permanently reducing the HP buffer.
lesson: Unless the relic payoff is clearly exceptional, favor the card removal option over losing max HP. A smaller HP pool makes every early elite and hallway mistake harder to recover from.
evidence_points: The Neow choice reduced maximum HP from 80 to 72 in exchange for a random rare relic, while card removal was available.
After the choice, the run fell to 29/72 after Lagavulin, 7/72 after the Sentries, and 16/72 by floor 13.
reasoning: The trajectory cannot establish that the relic was bad, but it does show that the permanent 8-HP reduction left a much smaller recovery margin during a sequence of damaging fights.

title: Use skipping more aggressively once the deck is functional
situation: When HP is already critically low or a reward is only situationally useful, especially after several rewards have been taken, skip rather than adding another mediocre card.
lesson: Prioritize high-impact scaling, consistency, or essential defense; otherwise skip. In particular, avoid continuing to grow the deck during a low-HP Act 1 unless the offered card directly solves the upcoming threats.
evidence_points: The run took Thunderclap at 29/72 HP and Clothesline at 7/72 HP, then continued taking Shrug It Off, Body Slam, Iron Wave, another Pommel Strike, and Evolve later in the act.
The final deck contained 20 cards, including 11 permanent nonstarter additions and two copies of Pommel Strike.
reasoning: The exact quality of each individual pick is context-dependent, but the repeated additions—many made while badly injured—produced a full 20-card deck without clear evidence that each reward was necessary for immediate survival.

title: Treat a low-HP run as a recovery problem before the boss
situation: When HP has already dropped into the danger zone and a boss or elite remains, take the first available rest that meaningfully improves survival rather than assuming later recovery will be sufficient.
lesson: After a damaging elite or a sequence of low-HP fights, switch the plan to survival: rest whenever a suitable campfire is available and preserve enough HP to survive multiple boss turns.
evidence_points: The run reached 29/72 after Lagavulin, 1/72 after the Sentries, and 16/72 on floor 13.
The only logged rest decision was on floor 15 at 22/72; the Guardian combat then began at 43/72 and still ended with the player at 10/72.
reasoning: Resting immediately before the boss was beneficial, but the repeated low-HP states show that the run had very little margin even after that recovery. Earlier recovery opportunities, when available, should be valued more highly than marginal upgrades.

title: Do not take unnecessary curses for gold
situation: When an event offers a large gold reward plus a curse, especially when already carrying substantial gold and no immediate purchase is required.
lesson: Prefer the safer gold option or leave rather than adding Regret for extra money. The curse can repeatedly pollute future hands, and the extra gold is only valuable if it enables a concrete near-term purchase.
evidence_points: At Floor 13, the run had 216 gold and chose Desecrate for 275 gold while becoming cursed with Regret; Pray for 100 gold and Leave were available.
The final 18-card deck contained Regret, and Regret was present in the Hexaghost hand on Turn 9.
The run later had 501 gold but no recorded shop decision before the boss.
reasoning: The event converted an already-healthy gold position into a permanent deck liability without recorded evidence that the additional gold was needed. Regret appearing in the boss hand demonstrates the downside reached the most important fight.

title: Preserve a potion when the boss is close and the current fight is controlled
situation: Before the boss, when entering a normal encounter at high or full HP and the fight does not clearly require the last available potion.
lesson: Avoid spending the final combat potion on routine damage or tempo if the encounter is already manageable; retaining one potion gives a valuable boss-fight recovery or damage option.
evidence_points: The Gremlin encounter on Floor 12 began with the player at 80/80 HP, and Flex Potion was used during that fight.
The final run state showed no potions remaining.
Hexaghost reached 28/250 HP before the player died, so a preserved potion could at least have provided an additional boss-fight option.
reasoning: The potion use was not obviously necessary from the logged starting HP, while the boss was narrowly unfinished. This does not prove a potion would have won, but it supports treating potion conservation as a priority when approaching the Act 1 boss.

title: Prioritize an engine or draw card over repeated incremental attacks
situation: When the deck already contains several ordinary attacks and a card such as Dark Embrace is offered, particularly more than once.
lesson: Give stronger consideration to draw or scaling cards instead of continuing to add modest attacks. A compact deck with an engine is more likely to convert Power Through and defensive cards into reliable boss damage than a collection of standalone attacks.
evidence_points: Dark Embrace was offered at both Floor 1 and Floor 7, but the run chose Iron Wave and Power Through instead.
The final deck contained Sword Boomerang, Twin Strike, Headbutt, Iron Wave, and multiple other attacks, but no Dark Embrace or other recorded draw engine.
The final deck did contain Power Through+, showing that an engine card could have had supporting material to exploit.
reasoning: The final build accumulated several incremental damage cards while lacking a persistent draw mechanism. This likely made important boss turns less consistent, although the trajectory does not prove that taking Dark Embrace would have guaranteed victory.

title: Convert Guardian defensive turns into damage
situation: When a boss is defending, or when your current block already covers much of the visible threat, reassess whether additional block is actually more valuable than attacking.
lesson: Against the Guardian, do not spend multiple actions on block by default. On its DEFEND turn, use the opportunity to push damage or apply an important attack effect; on attack turns, avoid stacking excess block when attacks remain legal and the boss is still far from dead.
evidence_points: Turn 9 showed The Guardian at 122 HP with intent DEFEND, while Armaments, Iron Wave, Perfected Strike, and Bash+ were all legal; after Battle Trance, the agent chose Shrug It Off+ and then Bash+ rather than using a direct damage card.
Turn 10 began with the Guardian at 106 HP and block 9, while Strike, Pommel Strike, and Sword Boomerang were legal; the agent instead played Shrug It Off followed by two Defends.
The combat ended with The Guardian still at 106 HP, despite the agent having reached the final logged turns with multiple legal attacks.
reasoning: These states show a repeated opportunity cost: energy was spent on additional block while the boss remained healthy and attack cards were available. The exact incoming damage is not logged, so this does not prove a particular attack would have prevented death, but it strongly supports prioritizing lethal progress over redundant defense in comparable states.

title: Skip more mediocre rewards instead of widening the deck
situation: When a reward does not clearly improve immediate damage, survivability, or an established synergy, especially after already taking several cards, prefer skipping to preserve draw quality.
lesson: Favor a smaller deck with a coherent damage plan over repeatedly taking merely playable cards. Before adding another card, identify what role it fills and whether it improves the upcoming elite or boss matchup; otherwise skip and let the existing strong cards appear more reliably.
evidence_points: The run took nine permanent reward cards across the listed CARD_REWARD decisions, while the final deck still contained only one Strike and one Perfected Strike as its explicit Strike-based damage core.

The final 15-card deck contained many separate one-off effects—Sword Boomerang, Iron Wave, Pommel Strike, Armaments, Intimidate, and Battle Trance—rather than a clearly concentrated scaling or damage package.
The Guardian remained at 106/240 HP in the final combat details after many turns, indicating that the accumulated card choices did not produce enough reliable boss damage.
reasoning: The exact quality of each individual reward is matchup-dependent, and later removals changed the deck, so this is not proof that any one pick was incorrect. The reusable pattern is to demand a clear role or synergy from future additions, because a broad collection of acceptable cards can still produce poor draws and insufficient boss damage.

title: Treat HP-loss events as a limited budget
situation: When an event offers upgrades or rewards for immediate HP loss while the run still has several combats before a safe rest.
lesson: Do not stack HP-loss events unless the resulting HP remains comfortably survivable; after taking one costly event, prefer preserving HP at the next event rather than paying another fixed loss for a marginal benefit.
evidence_points: Act 1 Floor 4: entered the random-upgrade event at 68/72 HP and chose the option that lost 14 HP, ending at 54/72.
Act 1 Floor 5: at 54/72 HP, chose the removal event and lost another 7 HP, reaching 47/72 before the next combats.
The next two combat summaries ended at 15/72 and 4/72 HP, forcing repeated rests and leaving very little margin for the Guardian sequence.
reasoning: The individual event choices were not immediately lethal, but their costs compounded with subsequent combat damage. A future run should evaluate the post-event HP against the number of upcoming fights, not just the immediate value of the reward.

title: At critical HP, compare marginal block with decisive damage
situation: During a boss fight when HP is already low and the hand contains a high-impact attack alongside several small block cards.
lesson: Before spending an entire turn on incremental defense, check whether a high-impact attack can remove or substantially weaken the immediate threat; when exact incoming damage is uncertain, treat this as a damage-race hypothesis rather than assuming more block is always correct.
evidence_points: Turn 5 of the Collector fight began at 38/82 HP with 3 energy and Fiend Fire legal, but the chosen sequence was Shrug It Off, True Grit, and Defend, ending the turn without an attack.
The following state showed HP still at 38 but only 6 block before Turn 6, and Turn 6 began at 6/82 HP after the enemy attack.
On Turn 6 at 6/82 HP, Clothesline was played on Torch Head while Collector remained at 175 HP; on Turn 7 the character reached 3/82 HP and ended with Torch Head still alive at 12 HP.
reasoning: The log does not expose exact incoming damage or prove that Fiend Fire would have been strictly superior, but it does show a defensive sequence followed by a severe HP collapse. In future boss turns, explicitly compare the survival value of available block against the possibility of ending the threatening enemy or advancing the boss damage race.

title: Stop adding marginal attacks once the core deck is online
situation: In Act 2, after acquiring a functional damage package and exhaust/block synergies, when the reward alternatives are mediocre attacks.
lesson: Prefer skipping weak or redundant attacks unless they solve a clear damage breakpoint; preserving a smaller deck is especially valuable when it already contains Fiend Fire, Feel No Pain, Dark Embrace, multiple Shrugs, and other established tools.
evidence_points: Act 2 Floor 25 offered Clash, Perfected Strike, or Iron Wave, and after repeatedly skipping that reward the run ultimately chose Iron Wave.
Act 2 Floor 29 offered Fire Breathing, Intimidate, or Twin Strike, and the run chose Twin Strike.
The final 29-card deck contained Iron Wave, Twin Strike, Anger, two Fiend Fires, and multiple other attacks, alongside the intended exhaust/block engine.
reasoning: The final deck already had substantial offensive density and useful exhaust synergies, so the later Iron Wave and Twin Strike additions were unlikely to improve consistency as much as retaining a smaller deck would. The reusable rule is to demand a specific role or breakpoint from late Act 2 attack rewards before adding them.

title: Treat low HP as the primary constraint
situation: After several combats have reduced HP substantially, especially when below roughly one-third of maximum, use available healing and prioritize survival over optional value.
lesson: Do not allow a sequence of fights to continue while critically low unless there is no safer alternative. When a rest is offered at low HP, healing should normally take priority over upgrading or other rewards.
evidence_points: The Act 1 event reduced HP from 80/80 to 64/80, and the next logged combat ended with HP 24/80; the following rest was used to recover.
HP was 14/80 before the later rest, only 9/80 by the Offering reward, and the Hexaghost combat ended at 3/80.
Act 2 began at 80/80 but fell to 62, then 48, then 27 across the next three combats before the loss.
reasoning: The repeated pattern is survival attrition across multiple floors, not a single catastrophic decision. Healing was taken when offered, but the run still entered later fights with too little margin, so future decisions should treat low HP as an emergency constraint and avoid extending risky combat chains.

title: Be more selective with duplicate attacks
situation: When a reward offers a card already represented in the deck, compare its marginal value against skipping rather than taking it automatically.
lesson: Prefer deck consistency over redundant additions unless the duplicate has a specific upgrade, scaling, or synergy purpose. In particular, reassess additional Iron Waves or Uppercuts when the deck already contains those cards.
evidence_points: Iron Wave was taken at Act 1 Floor 4 and then taken again at Act 1 Floor 12 when Iron Wave was again offered.
Uppercut was taken at Act 1 Floor 6 and then taken again at Act 2 Floor 18.
The final 23-card deck contains two Iron Waves, one upgraded, and two Uppercuts, alongside four Strikes and four Defends.
reasoning: The final deck contains several repeated attacks and a relatively large set of basic cards. The trajectory does not prove that every duplicate was harmful, but it supports a reusable rule to demand a concrete reason for duplicates so future draws remain more focused.

title: Use shops to buy attrition insurance
situation: When HP is already declining and a shop offers an affordable combat potion, value immediate fight assistance more highly than preserving excess gold.
lesson: Before a dangerous stretch, consider buying a useful potion if it is affordable and no stronger purchase is available; entering later combats with no stored potions leaves no recovery option when HP collapses.
evidence_points: At the Act 1 Floor 8 shop, HP was 48/80, gold was 61, and an Explosive Potion costing 48 gold was available, but the merchant was left.
The final build reports no potions remaining.
After Act 2 started at 80/80, three combats reduced HP to 27/80 before the final combat.
reasoning: The purchase was not guaranteed to save the run, and the exact route topology is unavailable, but the combination of declining HP, an affordable combat potion, and no final potion reserve supports treating potion purchases as insurance during attrition-heavy runs.

title: Treat optional HP costs as a limited resource
situation: When an event offers repeated HP loss or a maximum-HP sacrifice, especially before several unknown combats and with current HP already reduced.
lesson: Do not chain optional HP-loss rewards merely for gold or relic chances, and be especially conservative with maximum-HP sacrifices when current HP is not comfortably high. Preserve the HP buffer needed to survive the next fights unless the reward is clearly essential.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 4, the run chose Deeper three times, reducing HP from 74 to 62, then chose Gather Gold and fell to 51 HP.
At Act 2 Floor 22, the run accepted removing all Strikes for five Bites, losing 26 maximum HP; HP changed from 45/86 to 45/60.
After that event, the Act 2 Floor 23 combat ended at 13/60 HP, and the run eventually reached the Champ with only 66 maximum HP.
reasoning: These choices traded away both immediate and maximum survivability, and the subsequent combats repeatedly pushed the run into dangerous HP ranges. The exact counterfactual is uncertain, but preserving HP would have provided more margin for the later route and boss fight.

title: When low HP meets an attack intent, prioritize guaranteed block
situation: During a boss fight when HP is low, the enemy is attacking, and the hand contains playable block or block-generating cards.
lesson: Prioritize enough defense to survive the incoming turn before adding damage. At 9 HP against an attacking enemy, do not default to a damage-only play such as Whirlwind+ when True Grit is legal and can provide immediate block.
evidence_points: On Turn 9 against The Champ, HP was 29/66 and the intent was ATTACK; the run spent its 4 energy on Sentinel, Defend, and Bash, ending that decision with 10 block.
At the next logged state, HP was 9/66 and The Champ still had ATTACK intent.
With 9 HP, the legal alternatives included True Grit, but the chosen action was Whirlwind+.
reasoning: The logged states show a sharp HP decline between the attacking turn and the next decision, followed by another attack intent. Since True Grit was explicitly legal at 9 HP, a defensive action was available; choosing Whirlwind+ left no recorded block plan for the imminent attack.

title: Avoid paying twice for a card discarded for an event reward
situation: When an event asks for a card and the deck still relies on that card’s role, especially if replacing it later would consume gold.
lesson: Before surrendering a recently purchased combat card, compare the relic or event reward against the card’s replacement value and current deck needs. Avoid giving up an important attack unless the reward clearly justifies buying or finding it again.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 2, the run bought Carnage for 81 gold.
At Act 1 Floor 13, the run gave Carnage to the event in exchange for a relic.
At Act 2 Floor 24, the run bought Carnage again for 36 gold.
reasoning: The later repurchase demonstrates that Carnage remained useful, so the event trade created avoidable card churn and gold expenditure. The relic’s exact value is not recorded, so this is a conditional recommendation rather than proof that the event choice was strictly incorrect.

title: Take a late pre-boss heal when HP is only moderate
situation: At a campfire immediately before an Act boss, especially after taking damage from events or several fights.
lesson: Do not automatically smith at a late pre-boss campfire when HP is only around two-thirds full; take the rest if the next boss can plausibly remove most of the remaining HP.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 15, immediately before the Floor 16 boss, HP was 67/80 and smith was chosen instead of rest.
The Guardian combat began at 67 HP and ended with the player at 4 HP.
Earlier, the Gather Gold event had already reduced HP from 78/80 to 67/80.
reasoning: The run entered the boss without a substantial safety buffer, and the boss consumed nearly all remaining HP. The prior HP-for-gold choice made preserving the later campfire heal even more important.

title: Finish the Mystic before committing to the Centurion
situation: In the Centurion and Mystic fight, when the Mystic is weakened and the Centurion is defending or otherwise less urgent.
lesson: Continue prioritizing a nearly dead Mystic when it can be finished efficiently, then focus the Centurion; this reduces the chance of facing repeated debuffs or attacks from both enemies.
evidence_points: On Turn 4, the Mystic was at 19 HP and had a BUFF intent while the Centurion was attacking.
On Turn 5, the Mystic had ATTACK_DEBUFF intent and was reduced to 23 HP after Headbutt+.
On Turn 6, with the Centurion defending, the player used Bash+ and Wild Strike to kill the Mystic before continuing against the Centurion.
reasoning: The successful part of the final fight was removing the Mystic while the Centurion was not attacking. That target-priority pattern is reusable in similar two-enemy fights, though it still needs to be balanced against immediate survival.

title: Do not trade away a required key for convenience
situation: When pursuing a Heart-capable run and offered a relic in exchange for a colored key.
lesson: Treat the three keys as mandatory objectives; only take the relic instead when explicitly abandoning the Heart route or when the key trade is clearly necessary to survive.
evidence_points: On Act 1 Floor 9, Bag of Preparation was taken and the Sapphire Key was given up.
The final key state was ruby=False, emerald=False, sapphire=False.
The run therefore could not access the Heart route regardless of later combat results.
reasoning: Bag of Preparation was useful, but sacrificing the Sapphire Key permanently removed the possibility of a complete Heart victory. Key decisions should be evaluated against the run's actual win condition, not only immediate relic strength.

title: Do not attack into an unbreakable block after spending your energy
situation: When a zero-cost attack is available but the enemy has more block than the attack can remove, especially after all energy has been spent.
lesson: End the turn instead of playing an ineffective attack. On Guardian's turn 7, after Bludgeon+ reduced the boss to 52 HP, the boss had 20 Block and the player had 0 energy; playing Anger produced no recorded HP reduction.
evidence_points: Turn 7 began with The Guardian at 97 HP, 0 Block, and 3 energy; Bludgeon+ was played, leaving the Guardian at 52 HP.
The next logged state showed The Guardian at 52 HP with 20 Block and player energy at 0; Anger was chosen.
After Anger, the logged Guardian HP was still 52.
reasoning: The state sequence directly shows that Anger did not damage the boss because its block absorbed the attack. Ending the turn would have avoided an action with no immediate combat value and is a reusable rule for zero-cost attacks against blocked enemies.

title: Preserve defensive potions for the Act boss
situation: When a potion is the only emergency resource available and the current hallway fight is not threatening immediate defeat.
lesson: Unless it is necessary to survive the current encounter, save a defensive potion for the boss. The purchased Block Potion was used in a hallway Louse fight while the player had 65/74 HP, leaving no potions for The Guardian.
evidence_points: At floor 13, a Block Potion was purchased for 48 gold.
At floor 14, the potion was used against Louses while the player had 65/74 HP; the combat ended with the same 65/74 HP.
The final build lists no potions, and the Guardian fight ended with the player at 3/74 HP.
reasoning: The potion was spent outside the boss without preventing a net HP loss in the logged combat, while the later boss fight became a near-lethal race. Conserving that resource would have provided a stronger defensive option for the fight that ultimately ended the run.

title: Exploit frontloaded Neow blessings while preserving the advantage
situation: When Neow grants a strong effect for the next several combats, especially making enemies nearly dead, use those fights to build cards and resources without taking unnecessary damage.
lesson: Repeat the early-run pattern of taking advantage of the blessing while maintaining full HP; the free, low-risk combats are valuable for establishing the deck before harder encounters.
evidence_points: Neow's blessing made enemies in the next three combats have 1 HP.
The first three combat summaries ended with HP unchanged at 80/80, 80/80, and 85/85.

title: Prevent catastrophic HP loss in long elite fights

lesson: In extended encounters, spend defensive cards and available resources earlier once HP begins collapsing; a fight that leaves the character at critical HP has likely erased the value of the preceding route and rewards.

title: Start boss survival mode before reaching single-digit HP
situation: When fighting a boss and HP is already low while the boss still has substantial health, preserve defensive capacity before the hand becomes unable to block.
lesson: At low HP, evaluate turns primarily by whether they prevent the next damage cycle, using defensive cards and potions earlier when possible instead of relying on continued attacks to end the fight quickly. Treat debuffing or attacking as secondary when the boss is still far from death.

title: Do not trade substantial HP for random upgrades early
situation: When an early event offers random upgrades at a meaningful HP cost and the run is not yet stabilized.

title: Treat the five-Apparition event as a low-max-HP commitment
situation: When considering Apparitions while already carrying a moderately sized deck and expecting several difficult fights before the act boss.

title: Condition Spot Weakness on the enemy's intent
situation: When Spot Weakness is available alongside immediate attacks and the enemy is not attacking this turn.
lesson: Do not spend a turn on Spot Weakness when the enemy shows a defend or buff intent; use immediate strength or damage sequencing instead, and reserve Spot Weakness for an actual attack intent.

title: At critical HP, take immediate defense over setup
situation: When at very low HP and an enemy is attacking, especially with only one energy available.
lesson: Prefer a legal block or survival card over a strength or scaling card unless the setup action immediately prevents lethal damage. In the Collector fight at 4 HP with 1 energy, Ghostly Armor was available while Inflame+ was chosen; future play should preserve HP first in this state.

title: Treat large max-HP sacrifices as a commitment to flawless defense
situation: When considering a reward that removes a large amount of maximum HP in exchange for powerful defensive cards.
lesson: Accept the Apparition trade only when the deck and route can consistently exploit Intangible; after taking it, avoid spending turns on nonessential setup and treat even small HP losses as a major resource drain.

title: Skip marginal rewards once the deck is already crowded
situation: After the deck has established its main engine and a card reward is merely redundant or situational.
lesson: Use Skip more often to preserve draw quality and avoid adding cards that compete with the core engine. In particular, reassess duplicate powers and low-impact attacks instead of taking a card at nearly every reward.

The trajectory does not prove that every individual pick was incorrect, but it supports a reusable tendency to skip marginal or duplicate rewards once the primary defensive/exhaust plan is already present.

title: Stop repeating HP-loss event rewards when the run is fragile
situation: When an event offers multiple repeatable rewards at an increasing HP cost, especially with low current HP or no reliable healing.

title: Treat Coffee Dripper as a commitment to self-sustain

title: At critical HP, sequence engine cards and defense before marginal attacks

title: Never pass on available survival block at critical HP

title: Do not over-invest in setup while a damaging attack is available
situation: When HP is low, the enemy is attacking, and a damaging card is legal with the remaining energy.

title: Track the third key as an explicit objective

title: Do not continue several fights after reaching emergency HP

title: Preserve shop resources when already low on HP

title: Buy removal earlier when it competes with marginal power

title: Continue prioritizing the support enemy before the tank

lesson: Prioritize eliminating the support enemy when doing so is practical, even if the remaining enemy is tougher. Afterward, reassess whether the remaining enemy's next attack can be blocked before spending energy on extra damage.

title: Prioritize recovery when HP is already trending down
situation: At a campfire with substantially missing HP, especially before several remaining fights or a boss, compare the value of an upgrade against restoring enough HP to survive bad draws and unavoidable damage.
lesson: Do not default to smithing while wounded; take rest when the upgrade is not immediately essential and the run has already shown repeated HP loss. The goal is to preserve a meaningful HP buffer rather than repeatedly converting moderate HP into very low HP.

title: Be selective once the deck already has enough attacks

lesson: Prefer skipping over adding another merely playable attack when the deck is already large; prioritize cards that improve draw, scaling, or reliable defense instead of continuing to increase deck size.

title: Use emergency healing before lethal risk

title: Repeat early deck thinning followed by a high-impact purchase
situation: At an early Act 1 shop with enough gold for both removal and a strong standalone card.
lesson: Prioritize removing a basic attack when the deck is still starter-heavy, then buy a card that adds meaningful scaling or utility if the remaining gold allows it. This improves draw quality without requiring a large deck.

title: Exploit temporary early-combat advantages to preserve resources
situation: When Neow offers a blessing that makes the next several combats trivial and the early path allows normal rewards and shopping.
lesson: Use the temporary advantage to finish early fights at full health, collect card rewards and gold, and reach the first shop or upgrade without spending HP or consumables unnecessarily.
evidence_points: The agent chose the blessing making enemies in the next three combats have 1 HP instead of the alternative Neow rewards.
The first three logged combats ended with the player at 80/80 HP while defeating enemies with 1 HP.
The preserved health and early gold supported the Floor 5 Strike removal, Feed purchase, and Floor 6 Bash upgrade.

title: Treat the five-Bite event as a high-cost survivability trade
situation: When offered to remove Strikes and gain five Bites at the cost of substantial maximum HP, especially before difficult Act 2 fights.
lesson: Prefer refusing this event unless the run clearly needs the sustain and can tolerate the maximum-HP loss. Five added Bites can improve attacks, but reducing maximum HP sharply lowers the margin for unavoidable Act 2 damage.

title: At critical HP, spend energy on immediate multi-target impact or defense before setup
situation: When below roughly one-third HP and facing several attackers, particularly when an area attack or defensive card is already legal.
lesson: Do not spend the turn upgrading cards or sequencing delayed attacks if it leaves immediate damage or defense unused. In multi-enemy fights, prioritize legal AoE to reduce incoming threats, and at single-digit HP prioritize immediate block when it does not prevent a necessary kill.

The later sequence delayed available block while already at lethal-risk HP. Exact damage prevented by the alternatives is not logged, but both choices demonstrate a reusable priority error: low-HP turns should maximize immediate threat reduction rather than setup or delayed value.

title: Respect attack turns when block is zero
situation: When HP is already low, the enemy is attacking, and both defensive and offensive cards are legal.
lesson: Prioritize enough block to survive the incoming attack before continuing damage, unless the offensive line clearly kills the enemy or prevents more damage. In the final fight, at 39 HP with 0 Block and an attack intent, Defend+ was legal but Strike+ was chosen first.
evidence_points: Turn 12: the player had 39/90 HP, 0 Block, and the Bronze Automaton had Intent ATTACK; Defend+ and Strike+ were both legal.
The chosen line played Strike+ first, then Defend+, and only afterward played Feed.

title: Use skips more often after the deck has its core tools
situation: After obtaining reliable damage, draw, and defense, especially when a reward offers another situational duplicate rather than a major gap-filler.
lesson: Favor skipping marginal rewards to keep the deck compact and improve access to scaling and defensive cards. This run repeatedly added duplicates and finished with a 28-card deck, including two Pommel Strikes and two Shrug It Offs.
evidence_points: The run took Pommel Strike at Act 1 Floor 6 and again at Act 1 Floor 10; the final deck contains two Pommel Strikes.
It took Shrug It Off+ at Act 1 Floor 12 and again at Act 2 Floor 18; the final deck contains two Shrug It Off+ cards.
The final build had 28 permanent cards despite later removing Strike, Doubt, and Shame.
reasoning: The duplicates were not necessarily individually bad, but the final deck was substantially larger than the starting deck and contained several repeated effects. More selective rewards would improve draw consistency and make key scaling or defensive cards appear more reliably.

title: Repeat the curse-removal and scaling shop pattern
situation: When a shop offers both removal of an unwanted curse and a path toward scaling before the Act 2 boss.
lesson: Continue prioritizing removal of curses or weak cards while preserving enough gold for a meaningful scaling purchase. The run removed Doubt and Shame, then bought Inflame and later upgraded it, which helped create a credible boss-killing plan.
evidence_points: At the Act 2 shop, the run removed Doubt and bought Inflame for 72 gold.
At the later shop, it removed Shame, leaving the final deck without either curse.
The final deck included Inflame+ and J.A.X.+, and the Automaton was reduced from 300 HP to 4 HP.
reasoning: The shop sequence directly improved deck quality by removing curses and adding permanent strength scaling. The near-kill against the Automaton supports this as a strategy worth repeating, even though it was not enough to secure the run.

title: At critical HP, evaluate damage after enemy block
situation: When HP is near lethal and the enemy has substantial block, especially while attacking, compare each attack's actual post-block value against every available defensive option.
lesson: Do not spend energy on attacks merely because they are legal. If the attack will mostly be absorbed, prioritize block, mitigation, or a line that creates a real kill threshold; reassess this every action rather than committing to a damage sequence.
evidence_points: On turn 8, at 7/92 HP, Spheric Guardian had 47 block and Intent ATTACK_DEFEND; after Shrug It Off+ there were still Whirlwind+ and Metallicize+ available, but Whirlwind+ was chosen.
On turn 9, Spheric Guardian still had 38 block; Blood for Blood reduced it to 20, Bash+ reduced it to 10, and Strike+ was then played while the player remained at 7 HP and 0 block.
reasoning: The logged states show that the chosen attacks consumed energy while the enemy remained heavily protected and the player had no block. The reusable improvement is to calculate whether the next attack meaningfully penetrates block before sacrificing defensive tempo.

title: Treat Sozu as a major survivability tradeoff
situation: When choosing Sozu after Act 1, especially in a run already taking substantial combat damage, explicitly compare the value of future potion access against the immediate benefits of the alternative boss relics.
lesson: Do not select Sozu by default when the deck may need emergency healing, damage, or utility. If choosing it, compensate with a deliberately stronger defensive plan and avoid relying on potions that will no longer be available.
evidence_points: At the Act 1 boss reward, Sozu was chosen over Philosopher's Stone, Empty Cage, or skipping the relic.
After that choice, the final build had no potions, while HP fell from 92 entering Act 2 to 39 after Book of Stabbing, 24 after the Cultist fight, and 7 in the final combat.
reasoning: The trajectory does not prove another boss relic would have won, but it does show that Sozu removed a potential emergency resource during a run that repeatedly lost HP. Future decisions should account for that survivability cost rather than evaluating Sozu only as an energy relic.

title: Avoid redundant conditional cards without a clear payoff
situation: When a card is already represented in the deck, especially a conditional attack or a card whose value depends on a narrow combat state, require a specific synergy before taking another copy.
lesson: Prefer improving consistency or filling a missing role over repeatedly adding similar conditional cards. In particular, reassess duplicate Blood for Blood and duplicate defensive packages instead of taking them automatically from shops or rewards.
evidence_points: The Act 2 shop sold Blood for Blood for 38 gold, and it was purchased.

The following Act 2 card reward again offered Blood for Blood, which was taken; the final 27-card deck contains two Blood for Blood, two Shrug It Off, and two Metallicize cards, with one copy of each latter pair upgraded.
reasoning: The run accumulated several duplicate or overlapping effects while still reaching a 27-card deck and suffering heavy HP loss in successive fights. This supports using a stricter inclusion test for redundant cards so future draws contain more of the specific answers needed for the next combats.

title: Stop stacking optional HP and curse costs
situation: When an event offers an uncertain relic or modest reward in exchange for escalating HP loss or a curse, especially when the run is already healthy.
lesson: Do not repeatedly pursue escalating event rewards just because the success chance improves; leave once the HP risk is no longer justified. Likewise, prefer a non-curse option when the run does not urgently need the reward, because later curse removal consumes opportunities.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 3, the run chose Reach Inside and then Deeper four more times, paying 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 HP for progressively better but still uncertain relic chances.
At Act 1 Floor 14 and Act 2 Floor 25, the run chose relic/reward paths that added Regret and Decay curses rather than taking the available non-curse alternatives.
At Act 2 Floor 29, the run had to choose Drink specifically to remove all curses from the deck.
reasoning: These choices repeatedly exchanged survivability or deck cleanliness for optional value, and the later curse-removal event confirms that the curse costs remained strategically relevant. Future runs should stop escalating optional event risk unless the reward is necessary for survival or a clear build plan.

title: At critical HP, secure the immediate attack turn before utility
situation: When entering a turn at very low HP and an enemy has an ATTACK intent, evaluate every action by whether it immediately prevents lethal damage or meaningfully ends the threat.
lesson: Before spending energy on draw/exhaust utility such as Burning Pact, first ensure the available block is sufficient; if it is not, favor the strongest defensive line or enough damage to remove the attacker. Do not finish an attack turn with only small residual block unless the incoming damage is known to be safe.
evidence_points: The final combat began with the player at 14/80 HP against Centurion's ATTACK intent and Mystic's ATTACK_DEBUFF intent.
On Turn 2, after Burning Pact was legal and played, the player had 2 energy, then played Defend twice and ended with only 6 block while Centurion still had ATTACK intent.
The run ultimately died in that combat, with no later logged opportunity to recover.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not logged, so the lethal counterfactual cannot be proven. However, the recorded sequence shows that utility consumed energy before the attack was secured, and the final line produced only modest block at 14 HP; this is a strong warning to prioritize immediate survival in equivalent states.

title: Exploit Corruption and Runic Pyramid with exhaust and block density
situation: After acquiring both Corruption and Runic Pyramid, especially when the deck already has several skills that can be exhausted or retained.
lesson: Prioritize cards that improve exhaust, draw, or reliable block over adding more standalone attacks, unless a reward supplies essential scaling. This makes the Pyramid hand manageable and lets Corruption convert skills into efficient defense and energy-free plays.
evidence_points: The run took Corruption at Act 1 Floor 16 and Runic Pyramid as the Act 1 boss relic.
The final 22-card deck contains Burning Pact, True Grit, two Second Winds, Power Through, and four Defends alongside Corruption.
In combat, Corruption was played against the Act 2 Chosen, while Burning Pact, Second Wind, True Grit, and Power Through were repeatedly used in later fights.
reasoning: The run demonstrated that the exhaust package was active and compatible with Pyramid, but it also continued adding several attacks such as Heavy Blade+, Rampage+, Disarm+, and Pommel Strike. Future rewards should more deliberately reinforce the established exhaust/block engine so the deck has more consistent defensive turns before the boss.

title: Do not take avoidable curses when survival is already adequate
situation: When offered a curse-plus-relic option while near full HP and there is a healing alternative, especially before several upcoming combats.
lesson: Prefer the immediate healing option unless the relic is clearly worth the curse. A curse that must later be removed consumes gold and a shop opportunity, while the extra HP provides a safer buffer for the next fights.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 5, HP was 68/80 and the choices were healing 26 HP, gaining 5 Max HP, or obtaining a relic while becoming cursed with Regret; the run chose the curse option.
At Act 1 Floor 11, the run spent 50 gold specifically to remove Regret.
reasoning: The run had meaningful HP available to recover immediately, but instead added a curse and later paid to remove it. This created both a deck burden and an economic cost before the Act 1 boss.

title: Stop adding redundant attacks once the deck already has damage
situation: When the deck already contains several attack cards and a reward offers another similar, low-scaling attack without solving a current weakness.
lesson: Skip more often and prioritize cards that improve scaling, card flow, or reliable defense. Avoid accumulating multiple copies of mediocre attacks merely because they are immediately playable.
evidence_points: The final deck had 38 cards and included duplicate Sword Boomerang, duplicate Bloodletting, duplicate Headbutt, and two Strike cards, alongside Cleave, Twin Strike+, Whirlwind+, and other attacks.
The run continued taking attack-heavy additions in Act 2 and Act 3, including Cleave, Sword Boomerang, Twin Strike+, and Whirlwind+, while also buying another Sword Boomerang at the Act 3 shop.
reasoning: The final deck was large and attack-dense, so additional similar attacks were likely to dilute access to the deck's stronger defensive and scaling tools. The reusable correction is to demand a specific role from each added card rather than taking redundant damage.

title: At single-digit HP, plan the whole survival turn before spending energy on damage
situation: When HP is already in lethal range and the enemy is attacking or will attack next, especially when the hand contains only limited block.
lesson: Treat survival as the primary objective: calculate the available block before committing to attacks, and avoid ending the turn with only a small amount of block unless the logged state establishes that it is sufficient. If the current hand cannot survive, identify that danger before using energy on marginal damage.
evidence_points: On Time Eater turn 8, the player was at 9 HP and used Sword Boomerang and Strike before playing Defend and Entrench, ending the logged sequence with only 7 block.

On turn 9, the player remained at 9 HP with Time Eater intending ATTACK, played Defend for 7 block, then used Rampage+ and Strike and ended the turn while Bloodletting and Bloodletting+ were still legal.
reasoning: The sequence shows the combat reaching a point where the player had almost no margin for an incoming attack and was still spending actions on damage. Exact incoming damage is unavailable, so the precise counterfactual is uncertain, but the reusable issue is failing to establish a clearly safe defensive state before committing to attacks.

title: Prepare for the imminent boss before taking an optional key
situation: At a campfire directly before an act boss, when HP is meaningfully below maximum and the key can be obtained elsewhere.
lesson: Prefer rest or a high-impact smith over taking the key if entering the boss at reduced HP would create a narrow survival margin. Optional keys should not displace immediate boss preparation unless the run is already healthy enough.
evidence_points: Act 1 Floor 15: at 59/80 HP, the alternatives were rest, smith, or recall, and recall for the Ruby Key was chosen.
Act 1 Floor 16: the Hexaghost combat started at 59/80 and ended at 7/80 HP.
reasoning: The key decision occurred immediately before the boss, so the opportunity cost was direct: the run entered Hexaghost with 21 HP less than maximum and finished the fight nearly dead. Taking the key may be correct for a Heart attempt, but this state shows that boss preparation should take priority when the health buffer is poor.

title: Use death insurance when an attack can leave you at one hit point
situation: At low HP during an enemy attack turn, especially when the hand cannot produce enough block and a Fairy in a Bottle is still legally available.
lesson: Do not casually end a turn in lethal range. Spend the remaining defensive option or activate available death insurance before accepting the attack; preserving one extra turn is more valuable than saving a potion when survival is uncertain.
evidence_points: Collector fight, Turn 5: at 31/90 HP with the Collector attacking, the player had 16 block, 1 energy, and Fairy in a Bottle was a legal alternative, but chose End turn.
Collector fight, Turn 6: the next logged state was 1/90 HP, showing that the previous attack consumed almost the entire remaining health buffer.
Collector fight, Turn 6: after reaching 1/90 HP, the player still had to spend the turn on Shrug It Off+ rather than advancing the kill.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not logged, but the sequential states establish that ending Turn 5 converted a manageable 31 HP position into a one-hit-away position. The legal Fairy option was the clearest available insurance, and using it would have been preferable to preserving it while accepting a near-lethal attack.

title: Treat repeated long, damaging fights as a signal to change the combat plan
situation: When encounters repeatedly take many decisions and remove a large fraction of current HP, particularly before a boss or another difficult fight.
lesson: Shift priority toward shortening the fight and stabilizing defense rather than continuing the same damage-only pattern. Reassess target focus, block timing, and whether a high-impact attack or debuff should be used earlier whenever a fight is already consuming substantial HP.
evidence_points: Act 1 Floor 16 Hexaghost required 28 LLM combat decisions and reduced HP from 59/80 to 7/80.
Act 2 Floor 24 Book of Stabbing required 31 decisions and reduced HP from 50/80 to 7/80.
Act 2 Floor 25 Centurion/Mystic required 28 decisions and reduced HP from 23/90 to 4/90.
reasoning: This was a repeated pattern across difficult combats, not merely a Collector-specific failure. The later sequence of rests in Act 2 shows that the run was spending its route resources recovering from combat losses; future play should recognize the first such prolonged fight as evidence that the combat approach needs to become more efficient or defensive.

title: Prioritize attack coverage at low HP
situation: When HP is already reduced, the enemy intends to attack, and the current block is insufficient.
lesson: Choose enough immediate block before spending energy on attacks. In particular, at the Hexaghost turn with 35 HP, 0 block, 3 energy, and an ATTACK intent, Defend plus Shrug It Off was a legal safer line than spending the turn on Shrug It Off, Cleave, and Strike and ending with only 8 block.
evidence_points: Turn 14 began at 35/80 HP with 0 player block, Hexaghost intent ATTACK, and 3 energy; Defend and Shrug It Off were both legal alternatives.
The chosen sequence played Shrug It Off, Cleave, and Strike, then ended with 8 block while the enemy still had ATTACK intent.
The next logged state showed HP reduced to 29/80.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not logged, but the state clearly presented an attack threat and a legal way to produce more block. The resulting HP loss left less margin for the later boss turns.

title: Do not end with a playable combat card in hand
situation: When low on HP and a direct damage or debuff card remains legally playable after a setup action.
lesson: Avoid spending the turn on additional draw/exhaust manipulation if it leaves a useful attack or debuff unused. On the final turn, after Defend and Burning Pact, Clothesline was still legal with 1 energy; play it rather than selecting Burn+ and ending the turn.
evidence_points: Turn 16 started at 18/80 HP with 3 energy and Clothesline, Burning Pact, and Defend in hand.
After Defend and Burning Pact, the state explicitly showed 1 energy and Clothesline as a legal alternative.
The agent selected Burn+ and then ended the turn with Clothesline still in hand while Hexaghost had 89/250 HP.
reasoning: At 18 HP, ending with only 5 block and leaving a legal Clothesline unused sacrificed immediate impact during a lethal-risk phase. The log cannot prove the precise counterfactual outcome, but it does show a concrete lost action.

title: Exploit guaranteed early-combat safety
situation: When an opening blessing makes the next several combats nearly risk-free.
lesson: Use the safety window to collect early rewards and improve the deck without spending HP. The chosen blessing reducing the next three combats to 1 HP was effective here and is a strategy worth repeating when offered.
evidence_points: The Neow blessing chosen was: enemies in the next three combats have 1 HP.
The first three combat summaries show Jaw Worm, Spike Slime and Acid Slime, and Cultist all being finished from 1 HP while player HP stayed at 80/80.
The shop was reached at 80/80 HP, allowing card removal of a Strike for 75 gold.
reasoning: The blessing directly converted the first three fights into safe opportunities, preserving health while still enabling rewards and deck improvement. This created a strong early position even though the later boss combat was mishandled.
